s: Chapter 7 is a meditation sung by David to the LORD concerning the words of Cush, the Benjamite. David takes refuge in the LORD, asks to be saved from pursuers who would tear his soul apart like a lion, and swears that if he has done wrong or repaid evil to one at peace with him, the enemy may overtake him and lay his glory in the dust. He calls on the LORD to arise in anger and judge him according to his righteousness and integrity, and asks that the wicked come to an end while the righteous are established. He describes God as a righteous judge who has indignation every day and who prepares weapons against the man who does not repent. That man's own mischief and violence fall back on his own head, and David closes by promising thanks and praise to the LORD Most High.

The LORD is David's God and refuge, called on to save him, arise in anger, awake, and judge according to David's righteousness. He is described as a righteous God who searches minds and hearts, is a shield for the upright in heart, administers judgment to the peoples, and has indignation every day. He is given thanks and praise as the LORD Most High.

David, the author of this meditation sung to the LORD concerning the words of Cush, the Benjamite, takes refuge in the LORD and pleads for deliverance from his pursuers. He professes innocence, saying he has not rewarded evil to one at peace with him, and asks to be judged by his righteousness and integrity. He ends by vowing to give thanks and sing praise to the LORD Most High.

David's pursuers are those he asks to be saved from, who he fears will tear apart his soul like a lion with no one to deliver. He calls them adversaries raging against him and asks the LORD to lift himself up against their rage.

l: unrepentant man (wicked person who is judged), Psalms, Chapter 7
s: The man who does not repent is warned that God will sharpen his sword, bend and string his bow, and prepare instruments of death and flaming arrows. He is pictured as travailing with iniquity, conceiving mischief and bringing out falsehood, and as digging a pit and falling into it himself. His trouble and violence return on his own head.

Chapter 8 is a psalm by David, addressed to the Chief Musician and set for an instrument of Gath. It opens and closes by praising the LORD, whose name is majestic in all the earth and whose glory is set above the heavens. The psalmist says the LORD has established strength from the lips of babes and infants to silence the enemy and the avenger. Considering the heavens, the moon and the stars, the psalmist wonders why the LORD thinks of and cares for man. The psalm answers that man has been made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor, and made ruler over sheep, cattle, animals of the field, birds, and fish.

The LORD is addressed as 'our Lord' whose name is majestic in all the earth and whose glory is set above the heavens. He has established strength from the lips of babes and infants to silence the enemy and the avenger, and he made the heavens with his fingers. He also made man a little lower than the angels, crowned him with glory and honor, and put all things under his feet.

Man is the subject of the psalmist's wonder, as the question is asked why the LORD thinks of him and cares for him. He is made a little lower than the angels and crowned with glory and honor. He is made ruler over the works of the LORD's hands, with sheep, cattle, animals of the field, birds of the sky, and fish of the sea put under his feet.

The heavens are described as the work of the LORD's fingers, containing the moon and the stars which he ordained. The LORD's glory is set above them. The psalmist considers them as the occasion for wondering about man's place.

Chapter 9 is a psalm by David, set to "The Death of the Son" and addressed to the Chief Musician, in which he thanks the LORD with his whole heart and tells of his marvelous works. David praises the LORD for upholding his just cause, rebuking the nations, destroying the wicked, and reigning forever on a throne of judgment. The LORD is described as a high tower for the oppressed who does not forsake those who seek him or forget the cry of the afflicted. David asks for mercy and to be lifted from the gates of death so he can declare praise in the gates of the daughter of Zion. The psalm ends with the observation that the nations fall into their own traps, and a plea that the LORD arise, judge the nations, and make them know they are only men.

The LORD is thanked and praised as the one who maintains David's just cause, sits on a throne judging righteously, rebukes the nations, and destroys the wicked. He reigns forever, will judge the world in righteousness, is a high tower for the oppressed, and does not forsake those who seek him. David asks him to have mercy, to arise, and to put the nations in fear.

The nations are rebuked by the LORD, and their name is blotted out forever. They have sunk in the pit they made and are caught in the net they hid. David asks that they be judged in the LORD's sight and made to know they are only men, and says those who forget God will be turned back to Sheol.
The wicked are destroyed by the LORD, and the wicked person is snared by the work of his own hands. They will be turned back to Sheol, along with all the nations that forget God.

David's enemies turn back, stumble, and perish in the LORD's presence. They are overtaken by endless ruin, and even the memory of the cities overthrown is said to have perished. David also describes those who hate him as causing his affliction.

The oppressed are promised that the LORD will be a high tower for them in times of trouble. The afflicted are not forgotten, and the needy and poor will not always be forgotten nor their hope perish forever.

David gives thanks to the LORD with his whole heart, rejoices in him, and sings praise to his name. He asks for mercy, asks to be lifted from the gates of death, and says he will then declare the LORD's praise and rejoice in his salvation in the gates of the daughter of Zion.

Judgment is carried out and prepared by the LORD, who sits on his throne judging righteously and will judge the world in righteousness and the peoples in uprightness. He has already executed judgment and made himself known, and David asks that the nations be judged in his sight.

In Chapter 10, the speaker asks the LORD why he stands far off and hides during times of trouble, while describing how the wicked arrogantly hunt the weak. The wicked man boasts of his cravings, ignores God, speaks curses and deceit, and ambushes and crushes the helpless like a lion catching prey, believing God has forgotten and will never see. The speaker then calls on the LORD to arise, lift up his hand, and not forget the helpless. The speaker affirms that the LORD sees trouble and grief, helps the victim and the fatherless, and is King forever. The chapter closes with the hope that the LORD will hear the desire of the humble, strengthen their heart, break the arm of the wicked, and judge the fatherless and oppressed so that man of the earth terrifies no more.

The LORD is questioned for standing far off and hiding in times of trouble, and the wicked wrongly assume he has forgotten and will never see. The speaker calls him to arise, not forget the helpless, and break the arm of the wicked, affirming that he sees trouble and grief, helps the victim and the fatherless, hears the desire of the humble, and is King forever and ever.

The wicked arrogantly hunt the weak, boast of their cravings, condemn the LORD, and have no room in their thoughts for God. They speak cursing, deceit, and oppression, lie in ambush to murder the innocent, and believe they will never be shaken or called to account. The speaker notes they are caught in their own schemes and asks that the LORD break their arm and seek out their wickedness until none is found.

l: the helpless (victims of the wicked), Psalms, Chapter 10
s: The helpless are hunted, ambushed, caught in the wicked man's net, crushed, and made to collapse and fall under his strength. The speaker asks the LORD not to forget them, and affirms that the LORD helps the victim and the fatherless and hears the desire of the humble, with the hope that the fatherless and oppressed will be judged and terrified no more.

Chapter 11, attributed to David and addressed to the Chief Musician, is a declaration of trust in the LORD. David states that he takes refuge in the LORD and questions those who urge his soul to flee like a bird to a mountain. He describes the wicked bending their bows to shoot in darkness at the upright in heart, and asks what the righteous can do if the foundations are destroyed. The psalm answers that the LORD is in his holy temple and on his throne in heaven, observing and examining people. The LORD examines the righteous, hates the wicked and the lover of violence, will rain blazing coals, fire, sulfur, and scorching wind on the wicked, and, being righteous, will let the upright see his face.

The LORD is declared to be in his holy temple and on his throne in heaven, where his eyes observe and examine the children of men. He examines the righteous, hates the wicked and him who loves violence, and will rain blazing coals, fire, sulfur, and scorching wind on the wicked. He is described as righteous and as loving righteousness, and the upright will see his face.
David is credited as author of this psalm, written for the Chief Musician. He declares that he takes refuge in the LORD and objects to the advice to flee as a bird to his mountain.

The wicked bend their bows and set arrows on the strings to shoot in darkness at the upright in heart. The LORD hates them, and they are destined to have blazing coals, fire, sulfur, and scorching wind rained on them as the portion of their cup.

l: the righteous (the upright in heart), Psalms, Chapter 11
s: The upright in heart are the targets of the wicked, who aim to shoot at them in darkness. The question is raised of what the righteous can do if the foundations are destroyed, yet the LORD examines them and the upright are promised that they will see his face.

Chapter 12 is a psalm of David, addressed to the Chief Musician and set for an eight-stringed lyre. The speaker cries out to the LORD for help because the godly and faithful are vanishing, while everyone lies to neighbors with flattering lips and a double heart. The speaker asks the LORD to cut off flattering lips and boasting tongues, which claim that their own lips make them lord over themselves. The LORD answers that, because of the oppression of the weak and the groaning of the needy, he will arise and set them in safety from those who malign them. The psalm closes by praising the LORD's flawless words, trusting him to preserve them, and observing that the wicked walk on every side while what is vile is exalted.

The LORD is called on for help as the godly vanish, and the speaker asks him to cut off flattering lips and boasting tongues. He speaks in response to the oppression of the weak and the groaning of the needy, saying he will now arise and set them in safety from those who malign them. The speaker trusts him to keep and preserve his words from this generation forever.

l: godly and faithful (the godly man), Psalms, Chapter 12
s: The godly man is said to cease and the faithful to fail from among the children of men, which is the speaker's reason for crying out for help. Their disappearance is presented as the opening crisis of the psalm.

l: flatterers and boasters (the wicked), Psalms, Chapter 12
s: They speak with flattering lips and a double heart, and they boast that their tongues will prevail, that their lips are their own, and that no one is lord over them. The speaker asks the LORD to cut off their lips and tongues. The psalm ends noting that the wicked walk on every side while what is vile is exalted among the sons of men.

l: weak and needy (the oppressed), Psalms, Chapter 12
s: The weak are oppressed and the needy groan. Because of this, the LORD declares he will arise and set the oppressed one in safety from those who malign him.
The LORD's words are described as flawless, like silver refined in a clay furnace and purified seven times. The speaker affirms that the LORD will keep and preserve them from this generation forever.

Everyone is said to lie to his neighbor, speaking with flattering lips and a double heart. The speaker asks the LORD to cut off all flattering lips and the boasting tongue, and the LORD's pure words stand in contrast to this deceit.

Chapter 13 is a psalm attributed to David and addressed to the Chief Musician. David laments that the LORD seems to have forgotten him and hidden his face, and he asks how long he must carry sorrow in his heart each day. He asks how long his enemy will triumph over him. He pleads with the LORD, his God, to look, answer, and give light to his eyes so he does not sleep in death, and so his enemy and adversaries do not say they have prevailed or rejoice at his fall. The psalm ends with David declaring trust in the LORD's loving kindness, rejoicing in his salvation, and vowing to sing to the LORD because he has been good to him.

The LORD is addressed by David, who asks how long he will forget him and hide his face. David asks him to behold and answer, and to give light to his eyes. David trusts in the LORD's loving kindness, rejoices in his salvation, and says he has been good to him.

David is the author of this psalm for the Chief Musician. He laments that the LORD seems to have forgotten him, and he suffers sorrow in his heart every day while his enemy triumphs over him. He pleads for an answer and for light to his eyes, then declares trust in the LORD's loving kindness and vows to sing to him.
David's enemy is said to be triumphing over him. David prays that the enemy and his adversaries will not say 'I have prevailed against him' or rejoice when David falls.

Chapter 14, a piece for the Chief Musician by David, opens by describing the fool who says in his heart that there is no God, and declares that people are corrupt and no one does good. The LORD looks down from heaven on the children of men to see whether any understand and seek God, and finds that all have gone aside and become corrupt. The text asks whether the workers of iniquity have no knowledge, since they devour God's people like bread and do not call on the LORD. It says they are in great fear because God is in the generation of the righteous, and that they frustrate the plan of the poor, whose refuge is the LORD. The chapter closes with a longing for the salvation of Israel to come out of Zion, so that when the LORD restores his people's fortunes, Jacob and Israel will rejoice.

The LORD looks down from heaven on the children of men to see if any understand and seek God. He is the refuge of the poor, and the chapter ends with the hope that he will restore the fortunes of his people, bringing rejoicing to Jacob and Israel.

God is the one the fool denies in his heart, and the one whom people are said not to seek. He is described as being in the generation of the righteous, which causes the workers of iniquity great fear.
The fool says in his heart, "There is no God." The text calls them corrupt, says they have done abominable deeds, and says there is no one who does good.

The workers of iniquity are asked whether they have no knowledge, since they eat up God's people as they eat bread and do not call on the LORD. They are said to be in great fear because God is in the generation of the righteous, and they frustrate the plan of the poor.
The LORD looks down on the children of men to see if any understand and seek God. They are found to have all gone aside and together become corrupt, with no one doing good, not one.
God's people are eaten up by the workers of iniquity as though they were bread. The text expects that the LORD will restore their fortunes.
Israel is named in the closing verse, where it will be glad when the LORD restores the fortunes of his people. The verse also pairs Israel with Jacob in rejoicing.
The salvation of Israel is the object of a wish in the final verse: that it would come out of Zion. Its coming is linked to the LORD restoring his people's fortunes and to the resulting rejoicing.

Chapter 15 is a psalm of David that asks the LORD who may dwell in his sanctuary and live on his holy hill. The answer describes a person who walks blamelessly, does what is right, and speaks truth in his heart. This person does not slander, wrong his friend, or cast slurs against his fellow man. He despises a vile man, honors those who fear the LORD, and keeps an oath even when it hurts. He does not lend money for usury or take a bribe against the innocent, and the psalm promises that one who does these things will never be shaken.

The LORD is addressed in a psalm of David as the one in whose sanctuary and on whose holy hill people may dwell. Those who fear him are to be honored, and the conduct that qualifies a person to live in his presence is set out in the answer to the opening question.

The sanctuary, also called the LORD's holy hill, is the place the psalmist asks about when he asks who may dwell or live there. The unit gives the qualifications for those who may stay in it, and the one who meets them will never be shaken.

l: righteous person (who may dwell with the LORD), Psalms, Chapter 15
s: This person walks blamelessly, does what is right, and speaks truth in his heart. He does not slander, harm his friend, or cast slurs against his fellow man, despises a vile man, honors those who fear the LORD, and keeps an oath even when it hurts. He does not lend money for usury or take a bribe against the innocent, and he will never be shaken.

Chapter 16 is a poem attributed to David in which he asks God to preserve him because he takes refuge in the LORD. David declares that the LORD is his Lord and his only good thing, and he delights in the saints on the earth. He rejects those who give gifts to another god, refusing to offer their blood drink offerings or speak their names. He praises the LORD for assigning his portion, cup, and lot, which have fallen in pleasant places, and for giving him counsel. He expresses confidence that the LORD at his right hand will keep him from being moved, that his soul will not be left in Sheol, and that the LORD will show him the path of life and fullness of joy.

David, author of the poem, asks God to preserve him and says he takes refuge in the LORD, whom he calls his Lord and his only good thing. He delights in the saints, refuses to offer the blood drink offerings of those who serve another god, and blesses the LORD for counsel received even in the night. He sets the LORD always before him, is glad and secure, and trusts that his soul will not be left in Sheol and that he will be shown the path of life.

The LORD is addressed as David's refuge, Lord, and only good thing. He assigned David's portion and cup, made his lot secure, gave him counsel, and stands at his right hand so that he is not moved. He will not leave David's soul in Sheol or let his holy one see corruption, and he will show David the path of life, with fullness of joy in his presence and pleasures forever in his right hand.

l: inheritance (David's portion, cup, lot), Psalms, Chapter 16
s: The LORD assigned David's portion and cup and made his lot secure. David says the lines have fallen to him in pleasant places and that he has a good inheritance.

In Chapter 17, labeled a prayer by David, David appeals to the LORD to hear his righteous plea and to vindicate him, claiming his heart has been tested and found faithful and that he has kept from the ways of the violent. He asks the LORD to show loving kindness, keep him as the apple of his eye, and hide him under the shadow of his wings. He describes wicked enemies who surround him, are proud and callous, and are likened to a lion lurking in secret places. He calls on the LORD to arise, confront and cast down the enemy, and deliver him by sword and hand from men of the world whose portion is in this life. He ends confident that he will see the LORD's face in righteousness and be satisfied when he awakes.

The LORD is asked to hear David's plea, judge with equity, show marvelous loving kindness, and save those who take refuge by his right hand. He is also asked to keep David as the apple of his eye, hide him under his wings, arise, confront and cast down the enemy, and deliver David by his sword and hand. David says the LORD has proved his heart and visited him in the night, and that the LORD fills the belly of his cherished ones, whose sons have plenty.

David prays for a hearing and vindication, stating that the LORD has tried him and found nothing, that his mouth will not disobey, and that he has held to the LORD's paths and avoided the ways of the violent. He asks for protection from deadly enemies who surround him. He expresses confidence that he will see the LORD's face in righteousness and be satisfied when he awakes.

The wicked oppress David and surround him and those with him, closing up their callous hearts and speaking proudly with their mouths. They set their eyes to cast David and his company down to the earth. They are compared to a greedy lion or a young lion lurking in secret places, and are called men of the world whose portion is in this life.

The prayer is introduced as A Prayer by David and is offered as a righteous plea from lips without deceit. It asks for a hearing, vindication, protection, and deliverance from enemies, and it ends with confidence that David will see the LORD's face and be satisfied.

Chapter 18 is a song by David, the servant of the LORD, spoken on the day the LORD delivered him from all his enemies and from Saul. David praises the LORD as his rock, fortress, and shield, and recounts how the LORD heard his cry from the cords of death and answered with a storm-like descent of shaking earth, fire, darkness, hail, and lightning. The LORD drew David out of many waters and brought him to a large place, which David links to his righteousness and clean hands. David then describes being armed by God for battle, defeating and crushing his enemies, and being made head of the nations. He closes by blessing the living LORD, vowing to give thanks among the nations, and declaring that the LORD gives great deliverance to his king, to David and his offspring forever.

The LORD is praised as David's strength, rock, fortress, deliverer, shield, and high tower. He heard David's cry from his temple, came down in a fearsome storm, drew David out of many waters, armed him for battle, and subdued his enemies. He is declared the living God, unmatched by any other, who gives great deliverance and loving kindness to his king, David, and his offspring forever.

David, the servant of the LORD, speaks this song on the day the LORD delivered him from all his enemies and from Saul. He cries out in distress, is rescued, claims to have kept the LORD's ways, and is armed with strength, made head of the nations, and served by peoples he has not known. He vows to give thanks to the LORD among the nations and sing praises to his name.

David's enemies, described as strong, hateful, and too mighty for him, came on him in his day of calamity. With the LORD's help David pursued, struck, and crushed them like dust before the wind. They cried out but received no answer from the LORD, and foreigners came trembling out of their strongholds and submitted to David.

l: theophany (the LORD's descent in storm), Psalms, Chapter 18
s: In response to David's cry, the LORD bowed the heavens and came down amid a shaking earth, smoke, consuming fire, thick darkness, and thick clouds. He rode on a cherub on the wings of the wind, thundered with hailstones and coals of fire, and sent out arrows and lightning bolts. At his rebuke the channels of waters appeared and the foundations of the world were laid bare.

The LORD sent from on high, took David, and drew him out of many waters, delivering him from his strong enemies who were too mighty for him. He brought David into a large place because he delighted in him, and the LORD was David's support in his day of calamity. The song ends affirming that the LORD gives great deliverance to his king, David, and his offspring forever.

David claims that the LORD rewarded him according to his righteousness and the cleanness of his hands. He says he kept the LORD's ways, did not wickedly depart from his God, kept the ordinances and statutes before him, and was blameless, keeping himself from his iniquity. He ties this to the principle that the LORD shows himself merciful, perfect, and pure to those who are so, and shrewd to the crooked.

Chapter 19 is a psalm of David for the Chief Musician. It first describes how the heavens and expanse declare God's glory and knowledge day and night, with their voice reaching all the earth, and how God set a tent in them for the sun, which runs its course like a bridegroom or strong man with nothing hidden from its heat. It then praises the LORD's law, covenant, precepts, commandment, fear, and ordinances as perfect, sure, right, pure, clean, and true, more desirable than gold and sweeter than honey. Finally the psalmist says he is warned by them, asks to be forgiven hidden errors and kept from presumptuous sins, and prays that his words and meditation be acceptable to the LORD, his rock and redeemer.

The LORD is the one whose glory the heavens declare and who set a tent in them for the sun. His law, covenant, precepts, commandment, fear, and ordinances are described as perfect, sure, right, pure, clean, and true. The psalmist asks him to forgive hidden errors and keep him from presumptuous sins, and calls him his rock and redeemer.

The heavens declare the glory of God, and the expanse shows his handiwork. Day after day they pour out speech and night after night display knowledge, and their voice goes out through all the earth to the end of the world. God has set a tent in them for the sun.

The sun has a tent set for it in the heavens by God. It is likened to a bridegroom coming out of his room and a strong man rejoicing to run his course, going out from one end of the heavens and circling to the other. Nothing is hidden from its heat.

l: law of the LORD, Psalms, Chapter 19
s: The LORD's law is called perfect and restoring the soul, alongside his covenant, precepts, commandment, fear, and ordinances, which are described as sure, right, pure, clean, and true. These are said to be more desirable than gold and sweeter than honey, and they warn the psalmist, with great reward in keeping them.

David, author of the psalm, says he is warned by the LORD's law and that keeping it brings great reward. He asks who can discern his errors and prays to be forgiven hidden errors and kept back from presumptuous sins so he may be blameless. He closes by asking that his words and meditation be acceptable to the LORD, his rock and redeemer.

Chapter 20 is a psalm for the Chief Musician by David in which the speakers pray for a king in a day of trouble. They ask the LORD to answer him, send help from the sanctuary and Zion, remember his offerings, and grant his heart's desire and requests. The speakers declare they will triumph and set up banners in the name of their God. They affirm that the LORD saves his anointed and answers him from heaven with the strength of his right hand. They contrast those who trust in chariots and horses, who fall, with themselves, who trust in the LORD's name and stand upright, and they close by calling on the LORD to save and the King to answer.

The LORD is asked to answer in the day of trouble, send help from the sanctuary and support from Zion, remember offerings, accept the burned sacrifice, and grant the king's desires and requests. He is affirmed as the one who saves his anointed, answering from his holy heaven with the saving strength of his right hand. His name is the object of the worshippers' trust and the ground of their banners.

The king is the recipient of the worshippers' prayer, which asks that he be answered in trouble, set up on high, and granted his heart's desire and counsel. His offerings and burned sacrifice are to be remembered and accepted. The speakers state they now know the LORD saves him and will answer him from heaven. The psalm ends by calling on the King to answer when they call.

The speakers pray blessings on the king and vow to triumph in his salvation and set up banners in the name of their God. They declare their trust is in the name of the LORD rather than in chariots and horses. They say they rise and stand upright, and they cry out for the LORD to save and the King to answer them.

l: those who trust in chariots and horses (the enemies), Psalms, Chapter 20
s: They are described as trusting in chariots and horses rather than in the LORD. The speakers say they are bowed down and fallen, in contrast to the worshippers who rise up and stand upright.

Chapter 21 is a psalm of David for the Chief Musician that celebrates the king's joy in the LORD's strength and salvation. It recounts how the LORD granted the king's heart's desire, crowned him with fine gold, gave him long life, and laid honor and majesty on him. The king trusts in the LORD and, through the loving kindness of the Most High, will not be moved. The psalm then turns to the LORD's enemies, whom his hand will find out and consume like a fiery furnace, destroying their descendants because they plotted evil that cannot succeed. It closes with a call for the LORD to be exalted in his strength so that the people will sing and praise his power.

The LORD is praised for giving the king his heart's desire, a crown of fine gold, honor, majesty, long life, and gladness in his presence. His hand will find out his enemies and he will swallow them up in wrath like a fiery furnace, destroying their descendants and turning them back with drawn bows. The psalm closes by asking that he be exalted in his strength so the people can sing and praise his power.

The king rejoices in the LORD's strength and salvation, and receives his heart's desire, a crown of fine gold, honor and majesty, and life of length forever and ever. He trusts in the LORD and, through the loving kindness of the Most High, will not be moved. He is made most blessed forever and glad in the LORD's presence.

The LORD's enemies hate him and intended and plotted evil against him that cannot succeed. His hand will find them out, and he will make them like a fiery furnace in his anger, with fire devouring them. Their descendants will be destroyed from the earth, and they will be made to turn their backs when he aims drawn bows at their faces.

In Psalm 22, a psalmist identified as David cries out to God, asking why he has been forsaken and noting that God does not answer his groaning. He recalls that Israel's fathers trusted God and were delivered, while he himself is a despised worm mocked by onlookers who taunt that the LORD should rescue him. He describes his suffering through images of bulls, lions and dogs, bones out of joint, pierced hands and feet, and enemies dividing his garments, and he pleads for deliverance. The psalm then turns to praise: he vows to declare God's name in the assembly, and calls those who fear the LORD to glorify him because he has heard the afflicted. It closes by declaring that the ends of the earth and the nations will turn to and worship the LORD, whose kingdom rules over the nations, and that future generations will be told of his righteousness.

The LORD is addressed as God, holy, and enthroned on the praises of Israel, and the psalmist accuses him of being far off and not answering, even though he delivered the fathers who trusted him. He is asked to hurry to help and deliver the psalmist, and the psalm affirms that he has not despised the affliction of the afflicted but heard when the psalmist cried. His kingdom is declared to be his, with rule over the nations, and future generations will hear of his righteousness.

The psalmist, named in the heading as David, cries day and night to a God who seems to have forsaken him, describing himself as a worm, scorned, poured out like water, and surrounded by enemies who pierced his hands and feet and divided his garments. He recalls that God has been his God since birth, pleads for deliverance, and then vows to declare God's name and pay his vows in the great assembly because God heard him.

Israel is described as the people whose praises God inhabits, and its fathers are recalled as having trusted God, cried out, and been delivered without disappointment. Its descendants are called to glorify and stand in awe of the LORD.

The psalmist's enemies see him, mock him, insult him with their lips, and shake their heads, taunting that if he trusts the LORD, the LORD should rescue him. They are pictured as many bulls of Bashan, roaring lions, dogs, and a company of evildoers who pierce his hands and feet, stare at him, and cast lots for his clothing.

l: those who fear the LORD (worshippers), Psalms, Chapter 22
s: Those who fear the LORD are called to praise, glorify, and stand in awe of him, and the psalmist promises to pay his vows before them in the great assembly. The humble among them are promised that they will eat and be satisfied and praise the LORD, and that their hearts will live forever.

The nations are said to be ruled by the LORD, whose kingdom it is. All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to him, and all the relatives of the nations will worship before him, including the rich and those who go down to the dust.

Chapter 23 is a psalm attributed to David in which the speaker describes the LORD as his shepherd. The speaker says he lacks nothing, and describes being made to lie down in green pastures, led beside still waters, and guided in paths of righteousness. He states he will fear no evil even while walking through the valley of the shadow of death, because the LORD is with him and his rod and staff comfort him. The LORD prepares a table for him in the presence of his enemies, anoints his head with oil, and fills his cup to overflowing. The speaker concludes that goodness and loving kindness will follow him all his life and that he will dwell in the LORD's house forever.

The LORD is described as the speaker's shepherd who makes him lie down in green pastures, leads him beside still waters, restores his soul, and guides him in paths of righteousness for his name's sake. He is with the speaker in the valley of the shadow of death, comforting him with his rod and staff. He prepares a table before the speaker in the presence of enemies, anoints his head with oil, and fills his cup, and the speaker will dwell in his house forever.

The speaker, identified in the heading as a psalm by David, declares that the LORD is his shepherd and that he will lack nothing. He says he will fear no evil even when walking through the valley of the shadow of death because the LORD is with him. He expresses confidence that goodness and loving kindness will follow him all his days and that he will dwell in the LORD's house forever.

Chapter 24 is a psalm by David declaring that the earth and everything in it belong to the LORD, who founded it on the seas and floods. It asks who may ascend the LORD's hill and stand in his holy place, and answers that it is the one with clean hands and a pure heart who has not lifted his soul to falsehood or sworn deceitfully. That person will receive a blessing and righteousness from the God of his salvation, and is identified with the generation of those who seek God's face, even Jacob. The psalm then calls on the gates and everlasting doors to lift up their heads so the King of glory may come in. The King of glory is identified as the LORD strong and mighty, mighty in battle, the LORD of Armies.

The LORD owns the earth and all who dwell in it, having founded it on the seas and established it on the floods. He is the one who gives blessing and righteousness to those who qualify, and is called the God of salvation. He is also identified as the King of glory, strong and mighty, mighty in battle, and the LORD of Armies, for whom the gates are told to open.
The earth is declared to belong to the LORD, along with its fullness, the world, and those who dwell in it. It is said to have been founded by him on the seas and established on the floods.
The LORD's hill is asked about in the question of who may ascend to it and stand in his holy place. It is described as a place that only a person of clean hands and a pure heart may approach.

l: person who may ascend (the one with clean hands and a pure heart), Psalms, Chapter 24
s: This person is described as having clean hands and a pure heart, as one who has not lifted up his soul to falsehood and has not sworn deceitfully. He will receive a blessing from the LORD and righteousness from the God of his salvation. He is associated with the generation of those who seek God's face, even Jacob.
The gates, also called the everlasting doors, are commanded twice to lift up their heads and be lifted up. This is so that the King of glory, the LORD, may come in.

Chapter 25 is a prayer attributed to David, who lifts his soul to the LORD and asks for guidance, mercy, and deliverance. He asks not to be shamed or triumphed over by his enemies, and begs the LORD to forget the sins of his youth and to pardon his great iniquity. He describes the LORD as good and upright, one who instructs sinners and the humble and shows loving kindness and truth to those who keep his covenant. He says the LORD's friendship is with those who fear him, and that such people will dwell at ease with offspring who inherit the land. David describes himself as desolate, afflicted, and surrounded by many enemies who hate him cruelly, and the chapter ends with a plea for the LORD to redeem Israel from all his troubles.

The LORD is addressed by David as the God of his salvation, to whom he lifts his soul and in whom he trusts and takes refuge. He is described as good and upright, instructing sinners and guiding the humble, with paths of loving kindness and truth for those who keep his covenant. David asks him to teach and guide him, remember his mercy, pardon iniquity, pluck David's feet from the net, deliver him from enemies, and redeem Israel.

David, named as the author, prays to the LORD, declaring trust and constant waiting on him and asking not to be shamed. He asks to be taught the LORD's ways, to be pardoned for his great iniquity, and to be delivered from distress, describing himself as desolate and afflicted. He asks that integrity and uprightness preserve him.
Israel is mentioned in the final verse, where the speaker asks God to redeem Israel out of all his troubles. Israel is referred to as a single person ("his troubles").
David asks that his enemies not triumph over him. He says they are many and hate him with cruel hatred, and he asks the LORD to consider them and to deliver him.

l: those who fear the LORD, Psalms, Chapter 25
s: The text says the LORD will instruct the person who fears him in the way he should choose. Such a person's soul will dwell at ease and his offspring will inherit the land. The LORD's friendship is with them, and he will show them his covenant.

David asks the LORD not to remember the sins of his youth or his transgressions, but to remember him according to loving kindness. He asks the LORD to pardon his iniquity, which he calls great, and to forgive all his sins.

In Chapter 26, attributed to David, he asks the LORD to judge and examine him, claiming he has walked in integrity and trusted the LORD without wavering. He says the LORD's loving kindness and truth guide him, and that he has avoided deceitful men, hypocrites, and the assembly of evildoers. He vows to wash his hands in innocence, go about the LORD's altar, and proclaim thanksgiving and the LORD's wondrous deeds. He expresses love for the LORD's house, where the LORD's glory dwells, and asks not to be gathered with sinners and bloodthirsty men who are full of wickedness and bribes. He resolves to keep walking in integrity, asks for redemption and mercy, and says he stands on even ground and will bless the LORD in the congregations.

The LORD is asked by David to judge, examine, prove, and try him, and to redeem him and be merciful to him. His loving kindness and truth are said to guide David's walk, and his house is described as the place where his glory dwells. David vows to tell of his wondrous deeds and bless him in the congregations.

David appeals to the LORD to judge him, claiming he has walked in integrity, trusted without wavering, and avoided deceitful men, hypocrites, and evildoers. He vows to wash his hands in innocence, go about the LORD's altar, give thanks, and bless the LORD in the congregations. He asks not to be gathered with sinners and bloodthirsty men, and asks for redemption and mercy.

l: assembly of evildoers (those David hates), Psalms, Chapter 26
s: David says he hates the assembly of evildoers and will not sit with the wicked. They are described alongside deceitful men, hypocrites, sinners, and bloodthirsty men whose hands are full of wickedness and whose right hands are full of bribes. David asks not to be gathered with them.

David claims to have walked in his integrity and offers it as the basis for asking the LORD to judge him. He resolves to keep walking in it, and in the same verse asks for redemption and mercy. He states that his foot stands in an even place.

In Chapter 27, attributed to David, the speaker declares the LORD to be his light, salvation, and the strength of his life, so that he fears no one. He recalls that evildoers who attacked him stumbled and fell, and says he would stay confident even if an army or war came against him. He asks to dwell in the LORD's house all his days, expects to be hidden and lifted up on a rock in trouble, and promises sacrifices and songs of joy. He then pleads for mercy, guidance, and protection from adversaries and false witnesses, and states that even if his father and mother forsake him the LORD will take him up. The chapter ends with his confidence that he will see the LORD's goodness in the land of the living and an exhortation to wait for the LORD and be strong.

David, named as the author, declares that he will not fear because the LORD is his light, salvation, and strength. He asks to dwell in the LORD's house, seeks the LORD's face, and pleads for mercy, teaching, and protection from adversaries and false witnesses. He ends by affirming he will see the LORD's goodness in the land of the living and urging himself to wait for the LORD and be strong.

The LORD is described as the speaker's light, salvation, and the strength of his life. He is said to hide the speaker in his pavilion and tabernacle, lift him up on a rock, and take him up even if his father and mother forsake him. He is asked to hear, show mercy, teach his way, lead in a straight path, and not abandon the speaker, who calls him the God of his salvation.

Evildoers, adversaries, and foes came at the speaker to eat up his flesh but stumbled and fell. An army and war may still rise against him, and false witnesses who breathe out cruelty have risen up against him. The speaker asks not to be delivered over to their desire and expects his head to be lifted up above them.

The LORD's house, also called his temple, pavilion, tabernacle, and tent, is the place the speaker most wants to dwell in all the days of his life. There he hopes to see the LORD's beauty and inquire, and the secret place of the tabernacle is where the LORD will hide him in trouble. It is also where he will offer sacrifices of joy and sing praises.

l: trust and confidence in God despite danger, Psalms, Chapter 27
s: The speaker states that his heart will not fear and that he will be confident even if an army encamps or war rises against him. He bases this on the LORD being his light, salvation, and strength, and on the LORD's protection in the day of trouble. He closes by affirming he is still confident of seeing the LORD's goodness and by urging himself to wait for the LORD, be strong, and take courage.

In this chapter, attributed to David, he calls on the LORD, his rock, asking not to be met with silence lest he become like those who go down into the pit. He lifts his hands toward the LORD's Most Holy Place and pleads not to be drawn away with the wicked, who speak peace to neighbors while holding mischief in their hearts. He asks that they be repaid according to their works, because they do not respect the works of the LORD. The tone then turns to praise as David blesses the LORD for hearing his petitions, declaring the LORD his strength and shield. The chapter closes with a prayer that the LORD save his people, bless his inheritance, shepherd them, and bear them up forever.

The LORD is addressed as David's rock and is asked not to be silent or deaf to his cry. He is said to have heard the voice of David's petitions, and is called David's strength and shield, the strength of his people, and a stronghold of salvation to his anointed. He is described as one who will break down and not build up those who do not respect his works, and is asked to save, bless, shepherd, and bear up his people forever.

David cries to the LORD, lifting his hands toward the Most Holy Place, and asks not to be drawn away with the wicked or become like those who go down into the pit. He asks that the wicked be repaid for their deeds. After declaring that the LORD has heard him, he says his heart trusts in the LORD, he is helped, and he will thank him with song, then prays for the LORD's people.

l: the wicked (workers of iniquity), Psalms, Chapter 28
s: The wicked are described as workers of iniquity who speak peace with their neighbors while mischief is in their hearts. David asks that they be given what their works and the operation of their hands deserve. They do not respect the works of the LORD, and so he will break them down and not build them up.

The LORD's people are described as having the LORD as their strength, and he is a stronghold of salvation to his anointed. David asks the LORD to save them, bless his inheritance, be their shepherd, and bear them up forever.

David's petitions are a cry to the LORD for a response, made with hands lifted toward the Most Holy Place. They ask that he not be drawn away with the wicked, that the wicked be repaid, and later that the LORD's people be saved. David blesses the LORD because he has heard the voice of these petitions.

Chapter 29 is a psalm by David that calls the sons of the mighty to ascribe glory and strength to the LORD and to worship him in holy array. It then describes the LORD's voice on the waters, powerful and full of majesty, breaking the cedars of Lebanon, making Lebanon and Sirion skip like a calf and a young wild ox, striking with flashes of lightning, and shaking the wilderness of Kadesh. The voice also makes the deer calve and strips the forests bare, while in his temple everything says, "Glory!" The psalm closes by stating that the LORD sat enthroned at the Flood and sits as King forever, and that he will give strength and bless his people with peace.

The LORD is called on to receive glory and strength and the glory due his name, and is worshiped in holy array. He thunders as the God of glory on many waters, sat enthroned at the Flood, and sits as King forever. He will give his people strength and bless them with peace.

l: sons of the mighty, Psalms, Chapter 29
s: The sons of the mighty are addressed in the opening verses and commanded to ascribe glory and strength to the LORD. They are also told to ascribe to him the glory due his name and to worship him in holy array.

The LORD's voice is on the waters, powerful and full of majesty. It breaks the cedars of Lebanon, makes Lebanon and Sirion skip, strikes with flashes of lightning, and shakes the wilderness of Kadesh. It also makes the deer calve and strips the forests bare.
Glory is to be ascribed to the LORD, including the glory due his name, and he is described as the God of glory who thunders. In his temple, everything says, "Glory!"

Chapter 30 is a psalm attributed to David, headed as a song for the dedication of the temple. The speaker praises the LORD for raising him up, healing him, and bringing his soul up from Sheol so that he did not go down to the pit. He calls the LORD's saints to sing and give thanks, noting that the LORD's anger lasts a moment while his favor lasts a lifetime. The speaker recalls saying in his prosperity that he would never be moved, then being troubled when the LORD hid his face, and crying out for mercy and help. The LORD turned his mourning into dancing and clothed him with gladness, so that he vows to give thanks forever.

The LORD is praised for raising the speaker up, healing him, and bringing his soul up from Sheol. He made the speaker's mountain stand strong when he favored him, hid his face so that the speaker was troubled, and then heard his cry for mercy and helped him. He turned the speaker's mourning into dancing and removed his sackcloth.

David is named in the heading as the author of this psalm, a song for the dedication of the temple. The speaker, presented under his name, thanks the LORD for healing and rescue from the pit. He recalls that he once felt he would never be moved, was troubled when the LORD hid his face, and pleaded for mercy, then vows to give thanks forever.

l: anger and favor of the LORD, Psalms, Chapter 30
s: The text states that the LORD's anger is but for a moment while his favor is for a lifetime. It adds that weeping may stay for the night, but joy comes in the morning. The speaker experienced the favor as strength for his mountain and the hiding of the LORD's face as trouble.

l: mourning turned to dancing, Psalms, Chapter 30
s: The speaker says the LORD has turned his mourning into dancing, removed his sackcloth, and clothed him with gladness. The purpose given is that his heart may sing praise to the LORD and not be silent, and that he will give thanks forever.

Psalm 31, a psalm by David for the Chief Musician, is a prayer in which David takes refuge in the LORD and asks to be delivered from enemies who plot against him. He describes his distress, with wasting grief, sorrow, and sighing, and the contempt and slander of his neighbors and adversaries. He declares his trust in the LORD, saying his times are in the LORD's hand, and asks that the wicked and lying lips be silenced. He praises the LORD's goodness stored up for those who fear and take refuge in him, admits he once said in haste that he was cut off, and notes that the LORD heard his cry. The psalm closes by urging the saints to love the LORD and all who hope in him to be strong.

The LORD is addressed as David's refuge, rock, fortress, stronghold, and redeemer, the God of truth, to whom David commends his spirit and asks for deliverance. He has seen David's affliction, set his feet in a large place, and heard his petitions. He is praised for the goodness he has laid up for those who fear him and for hiding them from plotting and strife, and he preserves the faithful while fully recompensing the arrogant.

David, to whom the psalm is attributed, takes refuge in the LORD and prays for deliverance, mercy, and a shining face. He suffers grief, is shunned by neighbors, and is plotted against, yet declares "You are my God" and says his times are in the LORD's hand. He admits he once said in haste that he was cut off, but the LORD heard his cry, and he praises the LORD for marvelous loving kindness in a strong city.

David's adversaries lay a secret net for him, slander him, spread terror on every side, and conspire to take his life. Because of them he is contemptible to neighbors and acquaintances, who flee from him. David prays that the wicked be disappointed and silent in Sheol and that their lying, proud, contemptuous lips be mute.

l: saints and faithful (those who fear and trust the LORD), Psalms, Chapter 31
s: Those who fear the LORD and take refuge in him are said to have great goodness laid up for them, worked for them before the sons of men. The LORD hides them in the shelter of his presence away from human plotting and the strife of tongues. The saints are urged to love the LORD, since he preserves the faithful, and those who hope in him are told to be strong and take courage.

l: David's affliction and grief, Psalms, Chapter 31
s: David's eye, soul, and body waste away with grief, and his life and years are spent in sorrow and sighing. His strength fails because of his iniquity and his bones are wasted. He becomes a horror to acquaintances, forgotten like a dead man and like broken pottery, yet the LORD has seen his affliction and known his soul in adversities.

Chapter 32 is a contemplative psalm attributed to David about the blessing of forgiven sin. David describes how keeping silent about his sin made his bones waste away under the heavy hand of the LORD, until he acknowledged his transgressions and the LORD forgave him. He urges the godly to pray to the LORD while he may be found, and declares the LORD to be his hiding place who surrounds him with songs of deliverance. The LORD then promises to instruct and counsel, warning against being like a horse or mule that needs bit and bridle. The psalm closes by contrasting the many sorrows of the wicked with the loving kindness surrounding those who trust the LORD, and calls the righteous to rejoice.

The LORD does not impute iniquity to the blessed person, and his hand lay heavy on David day and night while David stayed silent. He forgave David's sin when it was confessed, is David's hiding place and preserver, and promises to instruct, teach, and counsel with his eye on the one he guides. He surrounds those who trust him with loving kindness and is the object of the closing call to rejoice.
David is named as the author of this contemplative psalm. The text attributes the psalm to him with the heading "By David."

The speaker recounts that while he kept silent about his sin, his bones wasted away, and his strength was sapped under the LORD's heavy hand. After he acknowledged and confessed his transgressions, the LORD forgave him. He calls the LORD his hiding place, expects preservation from trouble and songs of deliverance, and ends by urging the righteous to be glad and shout for joy.

l: godly (everyone who is godly), Psalms, Chapter 32
s: Everyone who is godly is urged to pray to the LORD in a time when he may be found. The psalm says that when the great waters overflow, they will not reach such a person.
The wicked are said to experience many sorrows. This contrasts with the one who trusts in the LORD, who is surrounded by loving kindness.

l: sin and iniquity (David's sin), Psalms, Chapter 32
s: David's sin weighed on him while he kept silent, causing his bones to waste away and his strength to be sapped. He then acknowledged it, did not hide his iniquity, and confessed his transgressions to the LORD, who forgave the iniquity of his sin.

Forgiveness is presented as the source of blessing: the person whose disobedience is forgiven and whose sin is covered is blessed. David experienced it when he confessed his transgressions and the LORD forgave the iniquity of his sin.

Chapter 33 calls the righteous and upright to rejoice in the LORD, thank him with the lyre and ten-stringed harp, and sing him a new song. It praises the LORD's right word, faithful work, and love of righteousness and justice, and says the heavens were made by his word and the sea's waters gathered by him. All the earth is told to fear him, since he spoke and it was done. The LORD overturns the counsel of the nations while his own counsel stands forever, and he sees all humankind from heaven, having fashioned their hearts. Kings and horses cannot save by army or strength, but the LORD's eye is on those who fear and hope in him, delivering them from death and famine, and the people close by declaring trust in him as their help and shield and asking for his loving kindness.

The LORD is praised as faithful in all his work, a lover of righteousness and justice, and one whose loving kindness fills the earth. He makes the nations' counsel come to nothing while his own stands forever, watches all people from his habitation, fashions their hearts, and considers their works. His eye is on those who fear him, and he is called the help and shield of his people.

l: those who fear him (those who fear the LORD), Psalms, Chapter 33
s: The righteous and upright are called to rejoice in the LORD, since praise is fitting for them. The chosen nation whose God is the LORD is called blessed, and the speakers identify themselves as people who wait for him, trust his holy name, and hope in him.

The psalm commands thanks to the LORD with the lyre and praise with the ten-stringed harp. It calls for a new song played skillfully with a shout of joy, and ends with the people's hearts rejoicing in him.

l: God's word and creation, Psalms, Chapter 33
s: The LORD's word is described as right, and by it and the breath of his mouth the heavens and all their army were made. He gathers the sea's waters in a heap and stores the deeps. Because he spoke and it was done, and he commanded and it stood firm, all the earth is told to fear and stand in awe of him.

The text says no king is saved by a great army and no mighty man by great strength, and a horse is a vain hope for safety. Instead the LORD delivers the souls of those who fear him and hope in his loving kindness from death and keeps them alive in famine. The people state that they have waited for him and trusted his holy name, and they pray for his loving kindness on them.

Chapter 34 is a psalm attributed to David, written for the occasion when he pretended to be insane before Abimelech, who drove him away. David vows to bless the LORD at all times, tells how he sought the LORD and was delivered from his fears, and invites the humble to magnify the LORD with him. He then teaches children the fear of the LORD, urging them to keep their tongues from evil, depart from evil, do good, and pursue peace. The psalm contrasts the righteous, whom the LORD hears, delivers, and protects, with those who do evil, whose memory the LORD will cut off. It closes with the assurance that the LORD redeems his servants and that none who take refuge in him will be condemned.

The LORD answered David, delivered him from his fears, and saves the poor man who cries out to him. His angel encamps around those who fear him, his eyes are toward the righteous and his ears hear their cry, and he is near to the brokenhearted and crushed in spirit. His face is against those who do evil, to cut off their memory from the earth, and he redeems the souls of his servants.

David is named as the author of the psalm, composed when he pretended to be insane before Abimelech, who drove him away. He vows to bless the LORD at all times, testifies that he sought the LORD and was answered and delivered from all his fears, and teaches children the fear of the LORD.

l: those who fear him (those who fear the LORD), Psalms, Chapter 34
s: Those who fear the LORD are encamped around and delivered by his angel, and they lack nothing, whereas young lions lack and hunger. The saints are urged to fear the LORD, and those who seek him will not lack any good thing.

The righteous are watched over by the LORD's eyes, and he hears their cry and delivers them out of all their troubles. Though their afflictions are many, the LORD delivers them from all of them and protects all their bones so that none is broken.
The LORD's face is against those who do evil, to cut off their memory from the earth. Evil will kill the wicked, and those who hate the righteous will be condemned.

Chapter 35, attributed to David, is a prayer for deliverance from enemies who pursue him without cause. David asks the LORD to fight for him, to shame and drive back his pursuers with the LORD's angel, and to let their hidden nets and pits catch them instead. He recounts that he mourned and fasted for these people when they were sick, yet they rejoiced at his adversity, gathered against him, and slandered him with false witness. He appeals to the LORD to stop looking on, wake up, and vindicate him according to his righteousness. He vows to give thanks in the great assembly and to speak of the LORD's righteousness and praise all day.

The LORD is called on to contend and fight for David, take up shield, buckler and spear, and send his angel to drive and pursue the enemies. He is praised as the one who delivers the poor and needy from those too strong for them, and David asks him to stop looking on, not stay silent or far away, and vindicate David according to his righteousness.

David, the author of this prayer, pleads for rescue from enemies who hid a net and dug a pit for him without cause, and who bring false witness against him. He says he mourned, fasted and prayed for them when they were sick, but they repaid him with evil. He vows to rejoice in the LORD, give thanks in the great assembly, and talk of the LORD's righteousness and praise all day.

David's enemies seek his soul, plot his ruin, hide a net and dig a pit for him without cause, and rise as unrighteous witnesses asking about things he doesn't know. They rejoiced in his adversity, tore at him without ceasing, gnashed their teeth like profane mockers, and spoke deceitful words, crying "Aha!" David asks that they be shamed, driven like chaff by the LORD's angel, and caught in their own net.

Chapter 36 is a psalm by David, the servant of the LORD, addressed to the Chief Musician. David first describes the wicked man, who has no fear of God, flatters himself, speaks iniquity and deceit, plots evil on his bed, and does not abhor evil. He then turns to praise the LORD, whose loving kindness reaches the heavens, whose faithfulness reaches the skies, whose righteousness is like the mountains of God, and whose judgments are like a great deep. The children of men take refuge under the LORD's wings and are satisfied from his house, for with him is the spring of life. David asks the LORD to continue his loving kindness to those who know him and to keep the foot of pride and the hand of the wicked from him, and he notes that the workers of iniquity have fallen and cannot rise.

The LORD is praised for loving kindness that is in the heavens, faithfulness that reaches the skies, righteousness like the mountains of God, and judgments like a great deep. He preserves man and animal, gives satisfaction from his house, and is the spring of life and the source of light. David asks him to continue his loving kindness and righteousness to those who know him and to the upright in heart.

David is named as the servant of the LORD and author of this psalm for the Chief Musician. He declares that a revelation within his heart concerns the wicked's disobedience, and he praises the LORD's loving kindness. He prays that the foot of pride and the hand of the wicked will not come against him or drive him away.
The wicked are called workers of iniquity, and David asks that their hand not drive him away. At the end of the unit they are described as fallen, thrust down, and unable to rise.

l: wicked man (the wicked person described in verses 1-4), Psalms, Chapter 36
s: He has no fear of God before his eyes and flatters himself too much to detect and hate his sin. His mouth speaks iniquity and deceit, and he has ceased to be wise and to do good. He plots iniquity on his bed, sets himself in a way that is not good, and does not abhor evil.

l: children of men (those who take refuge in God), Psalms, Chapter 36
s: The children of men take refuge under the shadow of the LORD's wings. They will be abundantly satisfied with the abundance of his house and made to drink of the river of his pleasures.

l: loving kindness (the LORD's loving kindness), Psalms, Chapter 36
s: The LORD's loving kindness is said to be in the heavens and is called precious. It provides the refuge under his wings that the children of men seek. David asks that it continue toward those who know the LORD.

Chapter 37, attributed to David, urges the reader not to fret or envy evildoers who seem to prosper, because they will soon be cut down like grass. It calls the righteous to trust in the LORD, delight in him, commit their way to him, wait patiently, give up anger, and do good. The chapter repeatedly promises that the humble and righteous will inherit the land while the wicked are cut off, their weapons turned against themselves. David says that in his long life he has never seen the righteous forsaken or their children begging for bread. It closes by affirming that the LORD upholds, helps and rescues those who take refuge in him, while transgressors are destroyed.

The LORD is the one the righteous are told to trust, delight in, commit their way to, and wait for. He establishes a person's steps, holds up the one who stumbles, knows the days of the perfect, and loves justice. He laughs at the wicked, breaks their arms, and cuts them off, while upholding, helping and rescuing the righteous and serving as their stronghold in trouble.

Evildoers, also called the wicked, are not to be fretted over or envied, since they will soon wither like grass and vanish like smoke. They plot against the just, gnash their teeth, and draw the sword and bow against the poor and needy, but their swords will pierce their own hearts and their bows will break. They borrow and do not repay, and one who once spread like a green tree passed away and could not be found. Their future is cut off and transgressors are destroyed together.

The righteous are told to trust the LORD, do good, wait patiently, cease from anger, and depart from evil. The LORD makes their righteousness shine like light, upholds them, and keeps them from falling, and they are satisfied in famine. They give generously, speak wisdom and justice, and keep God's law in their hearts. David has never seen them forsaken, and their salvation and refuge are in the LORD, who rescues them from the wicked.

The land is the inheritance promised repeatedly to those who wait for the LORD: the humble, the blessed, and the righteous. They will dwell in it, enjoy safe pasture, and live in it forever. Those cursed by the LORD and the wicked are cut off from it.

Chapter 38 is a psalm of David, written for a memorial, in which the speaker pleads with the LORD not to rebuke or chasten him in wrath. He describes severe suffering in his body and spirit, which he links to his sin and iniquity, and says friends and kinsmen stand far from him while enemies lay snares and speak deceit. He remains silent like a deaf and mute man, yet hopes in the LORD to answer him. He declares he will confess his iniquity and be sorry for his sin, notes that his enemies are many and vigorous, and closes by asking the LORD not to forsake him and to hurry to help him.

The LORD is asked not to rebuke or chasten the speaker in wrath, and is described as having pierced him with arrows and pressed his hand hard on him. The speaker hopes in the LORD to answer, and ends by pleading that he not forsake him or be far, but hurry to help as his salvation.
David is named as the author of this psalm, written for a memorial. He pleads for mercy amid suffering, confesses his iniquity, stays silent before his accusers, and asks the LORD for help.

l: speaker's sin and iniquity, Psalms, Chapter 38
s: The speaker says his iniquities have gone over his head like a burden too heavy to bear, and attributes his lack of bodily health to his sin and his wounds to his foolishness. He resolves to declare his iniquity and be sorry for his sin.

The speaker describes no soundness in his flesh or health in his bones, loathsome and corrupt wounds, burning in his waist, bruising, faintness, and a throbbing heart. His strength fails and the light of his eyes has left him, and he mourns all day, with pain continually before him.

The speaker's enemies seek his life, lay snares, speak mischievous things and meditate deceits all day. They are described as vigorous and numerous, hating him without reason and repaying evil for good because he follows what is good. He fears they will gloat over him when his foot slips.

Chapter 39 is a psalm by David, written for the Chief Musician and Jeduthun, in which David describes resolving to guard his tongue and stay silent before the wicked. His silence deepens his sorrow until his heart burns and he speaks to the LORD. He asks to know the measure of his days and confesses that life is brief, that every man is like a breath and a shadow, and that people busy themselves in vain, heaping up wealth without knowing who will gather it. He places his hope in the LORD, asks for deliverance from his transgressions and for the LORD's scourge to be removed, and acknowledges the LORD's rebuke. He closes by pleading for his prayer to be heard and for mercy, calling himself a stranger and foreigner with the LORD, as all his fathers were, so that he may recover strength before he departs and exists no more.

David resolves to watch his ways and bridle his mouth before the wicked, but his silence stirs his sorrow and his heart burns until he speaks. He asks the LORD to show him his end and the measure of his days, confesses his hope is in the LORD, and asks for deliverance from transgressions and removal of the LORD's scourge. He describes himself as a stranger and foreigner like his fathers and pleads for mercy so he may recover strength before he goes away.

The LORD is addressed by David, who asks him to reveal the measure of his days, deliver him from transgressions, and remove his scourge. He is described as the one who made human days handbreadths, who rebukes and corrects man for iniquity, consuming his wealth like a moth, and as the one in whom David hopes. David asks him to hear his prayer and not be silent at his tears.

Every man is described as standing as a breath and walking like a shadow, busying himself in vain. He heaps up wealth without knowing who will gather it, and when the LORD rebukes him for iniquity, his wealth is consumed like a moth. The text repeats that every man is but a breath.

l: human frailty and brevity of life, Psalms, Chapter 39
s: David asks to know how frail he is and says the LORD has made his days handbreadths, his lifetime as nothing before the LORD. Life is likened to a breath and a shadow, and the psalm ends with the prospect of going away and existing no more. This frailty is the basis of David's plea for mercy and recovery of strength.

In Psalm 40, a psalm of David for the Chief Musician, the speaker recounts waiting patiently for the LORD, who heard his cry, lifted him out of a horrible pit and miry clay, set his feet on a rock, and put a new song of praise in his mouth. He declares the blessedness of trusting the LORD and marvels that the LORD's wonderful works and thoughts toward us are too many to count. He says the LORD desired no sacrifice or offering but opened his ears, and he affirms that he delights to do God's will and has proclaimed the LORD's righteousness, faithfulness, salvation, loving kindness and truth in the great assembly. Yet he is surrounded by innumerable evils and overtaken by his own iniquities, so he pleads for deliverance and asks that those who seek his soul and mock him be shamed, while those who seek the LORD rejoice. He closes by calling himself poor and needy and asking his God not to delay.

The LORD heard the speaker's cry, brought him out of a horrible pit and miry clay, set his feet on a rock, and put a new song in his mouth. He is praised for wonderful works and thoughts toward us that cannot be counted, and for desiring not sacrifice and offering but opened ears. The speaker asks him to show tender mercy, deliver and help quickly, and not delay, and calls him his help and deliverer.

The speaker waited patiently for the LORD, was rescued from the pit, and was given a firm place to stand and a new song of praise. He says he delights to do God's will, has proclaimed God's righteousness, faithfulness and loving kindness in the great assembly without concealing them, and now, surrounded by evils and his own iniquities, calls himself poor and needy and pleads for deliverance.

l: enemies (those who seek the psalmist's soul), Psalms, Chapter 40
s: They seek the speaker's soul to destroy it, delight in his hurt, and say "Aha! Aha!" to him. The speaker asks that they be disappointed, confounded, turned backward, brought to dishonor, and made desolate by reason of their shame.

l: LORD's righteousness, faithfulness and salvation, Psalms, Chapter 40
s: The speaker says he has proclaimed the LORD's righteousness as glad news in the great assembly and has not hidden it in his heart. He has also declared the LORD's faithfulness and salvation, and those who love the LORD's salvation are to say continually, "Let the LORD be exalted!"

Chapter 41 is a psalm attributed to David for the Chief Musician. It opens by declaring blessed the one who considers the poor, whom the LORD will deliver, preserve, and sustain on his sickbed. David then asks the LORD for mercy and healing, confessing that he has sinned. His enemies speak evil of him, wishing for his death, while visitors speak falsehood and whisper that an evil disease has afflicted him, and even his own familiar friend has lifted his heel against him. David asks the LORD to raise him up, takes his enemy's failure to triumph as a sign of the LORD's delight, and closes with a blessing of the LORD, the God of Israel.

The LORD is said to deliver, preserve, and sustain the one who considers the poor, restoring him from his bed of illness. David appeals to him for mercy and healing, and credits him with upholding David in his integrity and setting him in his presence forever. The psalm ends by blessing him as the God of Israel from everlasting to everlasting.

David, the psalm's author, confesses that he has sinned and asks the LORD for mercy and healing. He describes enemies who wish for his death and a trusted friend who has turned against him, and asks to be raised up so that he may repay them. He concludes that the LORD delights in him because his enemy has not triumphed, and that he is upheld in his integrity.

l: he who considers the poor, Psalms, Chapter 41
s: He is declared blessed and is promised that the LORD will deliver him in the day of evil. The LORD will preserve him, keep him alive, bless him on the earth, not surrender him to his enemies, and sustain and restore him on his sickbed.

David's enemies speak evil against him and ask when he will die and his name perish. They visit and speak falsehood, gather iniquity, whisper together against him, imagine the worst for him, and say that an evil disease means he will rise no more. David says his enemy has not triumphed over him.
David's own familiar friend, in whom he trusted and who ate bread with him, has lifted up his heel against him. This betrayal is mentioned among the troubles David brings before the LORD.

David's illness keeps him on a sickbed, and his enemies call it an evil disease from which he will not rise again. David asks the LORD to heal him and raise him up, and the psalm says the LORD will sustain and restore the one who considers the poor from his bed of illness.

Psalm 42, a contemplation by the sons of Korah for the Chief Musician, is the lament of a speaker whose soul thirsts for the living God like a deer panting for water. The psalmist remembers leading crowds to God's house with joy and praise, and now weeps while adversaries taunt, "Where is your God?" From the land of the Jordan, the heights of Hermon, and the hill Mizar, the psalmist feels swept over by waves and billows and asks God, the rock, why he has been forgotten. Twice the psalmist addresses his own despairing soul, urging it to hope in God, for he will still praise him. The LORD is said to command his loving kindness by day, with his song accompanying the psalmist at night.

God is the object of the psalmist's thirst and longing, called the living God, the God of his life, and his rock. The psalmist asks why God has forgotten him, yet affirms he will still praise God for his saving help and presence.

The LORD is said to command his loving kindness in the daytime, and his song is with the psalmist in the night. This is the psalmist's expression of confidence amid distress, tied to a prayer to the God of his life.

The psalmist, writing as one of the sons of Korah's contemplations, thirsts for God, weeps day and night, and recalls once leading a crowd to God's house in joy and praise. Remembering God from the Jordan, Hermon, and Mizar while overwhelmed by waves, he asks God why he is forgotten and exhorts his own soul to hope.
The adversaries continually taunt the psalmist with the question "Where is your God?" Their reproach is likened to a sword in his bones, and their oppression causes him to go mourning.

l: despair and hope in God, Psalms, Chapter 42
s: The psalmist's soul is in despair and disturbed within him, and he confronts it with the same refrain twice: "Why are you in despair, my soul?" He answers it by commanding hope in God, declaring that he will still praise him as the saving help of his countenance and his God.

In Chapter 43, the speaker appeals to God to vindicate him and plead his cause against an ungodly nation and against deceitful and wicked men. He calls God the God of his strength, yet asks why God has rejected him and why he must mourn under the enemy's oppression. He asks God to send out his light and truth to lead him to God's holy hill and tents. He says he will then go to the altar and praise God on the harp. The chapter ends with the speaker questioning his own despair and telling his soul to hope in God, his Savior, helper, and God.

God is asked to vindicate the speaker, plead his cause, and deliver him from deceitful and wicked men. He is addressed as the God of the speaker's strength, as his exceeding joy, and as his Savior, helper, and God, and is asked to send out his light and truth to lead the speaker to his holy hill and tents. The speaker questions why God has rejected him but still resolves to hope in and praise him.

The speaker pleads with God for vindication and deliverance, and laments that he mourns because of the enemy's oppression and feels rejected by God. He asks to be led by God's light and truth to the holy hill and tents, vows to go to the altar and praise God on the harp, and urges his despairing soul to hope in God.

The ungodly nation is the party against whom the speaker asks God to plead his cause. It is mentioned alongside deceitful and wicked men from whom he seeks deliverance, and the enemy's oppression is the cause of his mourning.

Chapter 44 is a contemplative psalm by the sons of Korah, addressed to the Chief Musician. The speakers recall how God, by his own hand and not by their ancestors' sword, drove out nations and planted his people in the land, and they affirm that they trust God rather than their bows. They then lament that God has now rejected them, no longer goes out with their armies, scattered them like sheep for slaughter, and made them a byword and reproach among the nations. They protest that they have not forgotten God or broken his covenant, and they say God knows the secrets of the heart. The psalm ends with an urgent plea for God to wake, rise up, help, and redeem them for the sake of his loving kindness.
