God is recalled as having driven out nations and planted his people by his own hand, arm, and favor, and he is called King who commands victories for Jacob. In the present, he is accused of rejecting and shaming his people, not going out with their armies, selling them for nothing, crushing them, and hiding his face, while he is said to know the secrets of the heart. The speakers appeal to him to wake, arise, help, and redeem them for his loving kindness' sake.

The people, speaking as 'we' and 'I', recall that their fathers won the land through God and not their own sword, and they declare they will not trust in their bow. Now they are rejected, scattered among the nations, plundered, and mocked, yet they insist they have not forgotten God, been false to his covenant, or turned from his path. They are killed all day long, regarded as sheep for slaughter, and bowed down to the dust as they plead for help and redemption.

l: adversaries (enemies of God's people), Psalms, Chapter 44
s: In the past, the nations and peoples were driven out and afflicted by God so that his people could be planted in the land, and the speakers say God shamed those who hated them. In the present, those who hate the people take plunder, cause them to turn back, and taunt, reproach, and verbally abuse them. The enemy and the avenger are the cause of the speaker's shame.

l: national defeat and suffering, Psalms, Chapter 44
s: The psalm describes a present reversal: the people are made to retreat, are plundered, scattered among nations like sheep for food, sold for nothing, and made a reproach, byword, and object of head-shaking. They are crushed in the haunt of jackals, covered with the shadow of death, killed all day long, and bowed to the dust. The speakers stress that this came despite their faithfulness, and they attribute it to God's rejection and his hiding of his face.

Chapter 45 is a wedding song, set to "The Lilies," written as a contemplation by the sons of Korah for the Chief Musician. The speaker, whose heart overflows with a noble theme, recites verses for the king, praising him as the most excellent of men, blessed forever by God, and urging him to ride out victoriously for truth, humility, and righteousness. The king's throne is addressed as everlasting, and God, his God, has anointed him with the oil of gladness above his fellows because he loved righteousness and hated wickedness. The queen stands at his right hand in gold of Ophir and is told to forget her people and her father's house and to honor the king as her lord. The princess is led to the king in embroidered, gold-woven clothing with her virgin companions, and the speaker promises the king's sons will become princes in all the earth and that his name will be remembered in all generations.

The king is praised as the most excellent of the sons of men, with grace on his lips, and is called to ride on victoriously for truth, humility, and righteousness with sharp arrows that make the nations fall. His throne is declared forever and ever, and God, his God, has anointed him with the oil of gladness above his fellows because he loved righteousness and hated wickedness. He is attended by honorable women, will receive the princess and her companions, and is promised sons who will be princes in all the earth and a name remembered in all generations.

God is said to have blessed the king forever and, as "your God," to have anointed him with the oil of gladness above his fellows because the king loved righteousness and hated wickedness. The king's throne is addressed with the word "God" and declared to last forever and ever, with a scepter of equity.

The queen stands at the king's right hand in gold of Ophir, among the king's honorable women, who include kings' daughters. She is told to listen, consider, and turn her ear, to forget her own people and her father's house, and to honor the king as her lord so that he will desire her beauty.

The psalm is labeled a wedding song, a contemplation by the sons of Korah for the Chief Musician, set to "The Lilies." Its speaker recites it for the king, praising him, describing the queen and the princess's glorious procession with her companions into the king's palace, and promising that the king's name will be remembered and that the peoples will thank him forever and ever.

Chapter 46 is a psalm for the Chief Musician by the sons of Korah, set according to Alamoth. It declares that God is a refuge, strength, and ever-present help, so that his people will not fear even when the earth shakes and the seas roar. It describes a river that gladdens the city of God, where God dwells and helps at dawn, so that the city will not be moved. The nations rage and kingdoms are shaken, but God lifts his voice and the earth melts. The psalm calls people to see God's works, who ends wars, breaks the bow and spear, and burns the chariots, and records God's command to be still and know that he will be exalted among the nations and on the earth. The refrain that the LORD of Armies, the God of Jacob, is with us and is our refuge closes the psalm.

God is called a refuge, strength, and very present help in trouble, and is said to be within the city and to help it at dawn. He is named the LORD of Armies and the God of Jacob, lifts his voice so that the earth melts, makes wars cease to the end of the earth by breaking the bow, shattering the spear, and burning the chariots, and declares that he will be exalted among the nations and on the earth.

The city of God is gladdened by a river whose streams flow there, and is described as the holy place of the tents of the Most High. God is within it, so it shall not be moved, and God will help it at dawn.
The nations raged and the kingdoms were moved, but God lifted his voice and the earth melted. God declares that he will be exalted among them, and he ends wars to the end of the earth.

The earth is described as changing, with mountains shaken into the heart of the seas, and as melting when God lifts his voice. It is the place where God has made desolations, ends wars, and declares he will be exalted.

Chapter 47 is a psalm by the sons of Korah, written for the Chief Musician, that calls all nations to clap and shout to God in triumph. It proclaims the LORD Most High as an awesome, great King over all the earth who subdues nations and chooses Jacob's inheritance. God is described as having gone up with a shout and the sound of a trumpet. The psalm repeatedly commands singing praises, urging that this be done with understanding. It ends with God reigning over the nations on his holy throne, the princes of the peoples gathered with the people of the God of Abraham, and the shields of the earth belonging to God, who is greatly exalted.

God is called the LORD Most High, awesome, and a great King over all the earth. He subdues nations under his people, chooses their inheritance, goes up with a shout and trumpet sound, reigns over the nations from his holy throne, and owns the shields of the earth. He is greatly exalted and is identified as the God of Abraham.

The nations are commanded to clap their hands and shout to God with triumph. They are also described as being subdued under God's people, and God reigns over them. The princes of the peoples are gathered together with the people of the God of Abraham.

The psalm calls for clapping, shouting in triumph, and repeated singing of praises to God as King. It instructs that praises be sung with understanding. The grounds given are God's kingship over all the earth, his reign over the nations, and his great exaltation.

Chapter 48 is a song, a psalm by the sons of Korah, praising the LORD and his city on Mount Zion. It describes Zion as beautiful, the joy of the whole earth, and the city of the great King, where God has shown himself as a refuge. Kings assembled and passed by together, but on seeing the city they were amazed, dismayed, and trembling, and hurried away. The people reflect on God's loving kindness in his temple, and the daughters of Judah are called to rejoice at his judgments. The psalm closes by urging people to walk around Zion, count its towers, and tell the next generation that this God is their God forever and will guide them even to death.

The LORD is declared great and greatly to be praised in his city and holy mountain. He has shown himself as a refuge in Zion's citadels, breaks the ships of Tarshish with the east wind, and will establish the city forever. His name and praise reach the ends of the earth, his right hand is full of righteousness, and he is called the God who will guide his people even to death.

Mount Zion is described as beautiful in elevation, the joy of the whole earth, on the north sides, and the city of the great King. It is the place where God is a refuge, where his temple stands, and which God will establish forever. Its towers, bulwarks, and palaces are to be examined so the next generation can be told of it, and it is called to be glad.

The kings assembled themselves and passed by together. When they saw the city they were amazed and dismayed, and they hurried away. Trembling took hold of them, with pain like that of a woman in labor.

Chapter 49 is a psalm by the sons of Korah, addressed to all peoples of the world, in which the psalmist speaks wisdom and a riddle on the harp. The psalmist asks why he should fear evil days, and he turns to those who trust in their wealth. No one can redeem another or pay God a ransom, because the price of life is too costly and wise and foolish alike die and leave their wealth to others. The rich and foolish are likened to animals that perish, appointed as a flock for Sheol with Death as their shepherd. The psalmist expects God to redeem his soul from Sheol and receive him, and urges listeners not to fear the rich, since a man carries nothing away at death and goes to the generation of his fathers.
God is the one to whom no man can give a ransom for his brother. The psalmist declares that God will redeem his soul from the power of Sheol and receive him.
Sheol is the place where the foolish are appointed like a flock, and where their beauty will decay far from their mansions. The psalmist says God will redeem his soul from its power.
Death is described as the shepherd of the foolish, who are appointed as a flock for Sheol. The upright are said to have dominion over them in the morning.

l: psalmist (speaker of the Psalm), Psalms, Chapter 49
s: The psalmist calls all peoples to listen and says his mouth will speak wisdom and his heart understanding. He will incline his ear to a proverb and solve his riddle on the harp, asks why he should fear evil days, and states that God will redeem his soul from Sheol and receive him.

l: peoples (all inhabitants of the world), Psalms, Chapter 49
s: The peoples are addressed as the audience of the psalm, low and high, rich and poor together. They are called to hear the psalmist's wisdom.

l: rich who trust in wealth, Psalms, Chapter 49
s: Those who trust in their wealth and boast of their riches cannot redeem a brother or ransom him from God. They think their houses will endure forever and name lands after themselves, yet they die, leave their wealth to others, go to the generation of their fathers, and never see the light. A man with riches but no understanding is like the animals that perish.
Wealth cannot buy life or redemption, and it is left to others when its owner dies. A man carries nothing away at death, and his glory does not descend after him.

The redemption of life is said to be costly, and no payment is ever enough to let someone live forever and not see corruption. No one can give God a ransom for his brother, yet God will redeem the psalmist's soul from Sheol.

l: fool and the senseless, Psalms, Chapter 49
s: The fool and the senseless perish just as wise men die, and leave their wealth to others. Their destiny, shared by those who approve their sayings, is to be a flock for Sheol with Death as shepherd.

Psalm 50, a psalm of Asaph, depicts God, the Mighty One, speaking from Zion and summoning heaven and earth to witness as he judges his people. He addresses Israel, saying he does not rebuke their sacrifices but has no need of them, since every animal and the whole world already belong to him. He calls them instead to offer the sacrifice of thanksgiving, pay their vows to the Most High, and call on him in trouble. He then turns to the wicked, who recite his statutes while hating instruction, consenting to thieves, joining adulterers, and practicing deceit and slander against their own kin. God warns that his past silence was misread as likeness to them, and that he will rebuke and tear apart those who forget him, while the one who offers thanksgiving glorifies him and will see his salvation.

God, the Mighty One, speaks and calls the earth from sunrise to sunset, shining out of Zion, coming with devouring fire and storm, and summoning heaven and earth to judge his people. He declares that he needs no sacrifices because all creatures and the world are his, and he asks for thanksgiving, vows paid, and calling on him in trouble. He will rebuke the wicked who mistook his silence for being like them, and he promises salvation to those who offer thanksgiving.

Israel, addressed as God's people, is called to gather and hear God testify against them, 'I am God, your God.' They are told that their burnt offerings are continually before God and not rebuked, but that God does not need them. They are urged to offer thanksgiving, pay vows to the Most High, and call on him in the day of trouble, when he will deliver them.

The wicked are challenged by God over what right they have to declare his statutes and take his covenant on their lips while hating instruction and throwing his words behind them. They are charged with consenting to a thief, joining adulterers, giving their mouths to evil, framing deceit, and slandering their own brother and mother's son. God says he kept silent and they thought he was like them, but he will rebuke and accuse them, and warns he will tear them to pieces with no one to deliver.

l: sacrifices and offerings (of Israel), Psalms, Chapter 50
s: God says he does not rebuke Israel for their sacrifices and that their burnt offerings are continually before him. He states he has no need of a bull from their stall or goats from their pens, since all animals and the world are his, and he would not eat bulls' meat or drink goats' blood. The covenant with his saints was made by sacrifice, but the offerings are not what God ultimately wants.

God calls his people to offer the sacrifice of thanksgiving and pay their vows to the Most High as what he desires in place of animal offerings. At the close, whoever offers it is said to glorify God and prepare the way for God to show them his salvation.

l: judgment (God's judgment of his people), Psalms, Chapter 50
s: God calls the heavens above and the earth so that he may judge his people, and the heavens declare his righteousness because God himself is judge. The judgment includes testimony against Israel about sacrifices and a sharper indictment of the wicked for hypocrisy, complicity with thieves and adulterers, deceit, and slander. It ends with a warning of being torn apart for those who forget God and a promise of salvation for those who offer thanksgiving.

Chapter 51 is a psalm of David, written when Nathan the prophet came to him after he had gone in to Bathsheba. David pleads with God for mercy, asking to be washed and cleansed from his transgressions, which he acknowledges are constantly before him. He confesses that he has sinned against God alone, asks for a clean heart and a right spirit, and begs not to be cast from God's presence or have the Holy Spirit taken from him. He vows to teach transgressors God's ways and to praise him once restored, and states that God desires a broken and contrite heart rather than sacrifice. The psalm closes with a prayer for Zion and Jerusalem, after which righteous sacrifices and bulls on the altar will please God.

David, writing after Nathan the prophet came to him over Bathsheba, confesses his transgressions and pleads for mercy, cleansing, a clean heart and restored joy. He asks not to be thrown from God's presence and promises to teach transgressors God's ways and to declare God's praise.

God is addressed as the one against whom David has sinned, who is proved right when he speaks and justified when he judges. He desires truth in the inward parts, teaches wisdom, can cleanse and renew, and does not despise a broken and contrite heart. He takes no delight in sacrifice or burnt offering as such, but will delight in sacrifices of righteousness once Zion is favored.

David says he knows his transgressions and that his sin is constantly before him. He declares that he has sinned against God only and done evil in his sight, that he was born in iniquity and conceived in sin, and he asks to be delivered from the guilt of bloodshed.

David asks God to blot out his transgressions and iniquities, wash him thoroughly, cleanse him, and purify him with hyssop so that he will be whiter than snow. He also asks God to hide his face from his sins, create a clean heart, renew a right spirit, and restore the joy of salvation.

David says God does not delight in sacrifice or burnt offering, or else he would give it, and that the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit and a broken, contrite heart. The psalm ends with the promise that God will delight in sacrifices of righteousness, burnt offerings and whole burnt offerings, and that bulls will be offered on his altar.

Chapter 52 is a contemplation by David, composed when Doeg the Edomite told Saul that David had come to Ahimelech's house. David addresses a boastful 'mighty man' whose deceitful tongue plots destruction and who loves evil more than good and lying more than truth. He declares that God will destroy this man forever, pluck him from his tent and root him out of the land of the living. The righteous will see it, fear, and laugh, noting that the man trusted in his riches and not in God. David contrasts himself as a green olive tree in God's house, trusting God's loving kindness and promising to give thanks and hope in God's name before the saints.

David is credited with this contemplation, written when Doeg told Saul that David had come to Ahimelech's house. He confronts the boastful deceiver, then describes himself as a green olive tree in God's house who trusts God's loving kindness forever. He vows to give God thanks forever and to hope in God's name in the presence of the saints.

Doeg the Edomite is named in the superscription as the one who came and told Saul that David had come to Ahimelech's house. The psalm's address to a boastful, deceitful 'mighty man' with a destructive tongue is set against this event, and the man is said to face destruction by God.

God's loving kindness is said to endure continually, and David trusts it forever. God will destroy the deceitful man forever, taking him up, plucking him from his tent and rooting him out of the land of the living. David thanks God for having done it and hopes in his name, which he calls good.
